newsitem.title: INDIA: India rules out equipment failures in air disaster.
newsitem.headline: India rules out equipment failures in air disaster.

text.p: India said on Wednesday it ruled out the possibilities that outdated equipment or language problems could have caused the world's worst mid-air collision in which some 350 people were killed.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda appealed for a suspension of judgement on India's worst air disaster as top civil aviation officials said only analysis of the so-called "black boxes" of the two aircraft would determine what went wrong.
A Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin IL-76 freighter collided on Tuesday evening some 80 km (50 miles) west of Delhi.
There were no survivors among the 312 people aboard the Saudi jumbo that had just taken off from New Delhi or among the 37 people on the KazAir freighter that was preparing to land.
Indian aviation officials said they would not guess what went wrong, but said the problem was not associated with language or outdated equipment.
India has said it will appoint a high court judge to investigate the collision.
"Until the report is available, it cannot be said whether it was failure of pilots or the air traffic control," Deve Gowda told reporters at the crash site at Charkhi Dadri.
Speculation on the cause of the collision had ranged from inadequate equipment at New Delhi airport to pilot misunderstanding of instructions from ground controllers.
Aviation officials said the transcript of the final exchange between the pilots of the two airliners and the ground controllers showed that both pilots had understood the ground instructions clearly.

"It is clear that the Kazakhstan airline knew it was to fly at 15,000 feet, that Saudi Arabia was cleared to fly to 14,000, and that the distance between them was 1,000 feet, which is the standard," Yogesh Chandra, the top civil servant at the Civil Aviation Ministry told a news conference.
He said it was also clear "that both the planes were aware of each other's approach, especially the Kazakhstan airliner, which asked what is the distance now between us".
"What the pilots did after this exchange of conversation is something that can only come out once the black boxes are decoded," Chandra added.
Asked what could have gone wrong, Chandra said: "The black boxes will now reveal that. I am sorry, I cannot conjecture."
Speculation that the equipment at New Delhi airport was inadequate was "absolutely incorrect", Chandra said.

Attention has also focused on the fact that planes landing and taking off from Delhi's Indira Gandhi airport use the same corridor, but Chandra suggested this was not a potential cause of the collision.
Using a single corridor was normal in many countries, he said.
"If there are double or triple or four runways, an accident is an accident is an accident," Chandra said.
"I live with this. Twenty-four hours a day we are praying that all our aircraft are on the ground."
Deve Gowda said earlier that if the judicial inquiry recommended the modernisation of the civil aviation system, this would be done, PTI reported.
It quoted him as saying that the government would not spare anyone found guilty, and that the recommendations of the inquiry panel would be implemented.
